newsitem.title: USA: Last U.S. Coast Guard ships leave Governors Island.
newsitem.headline: Last U.S. Coast Guard ships leave Governors Island.

text.p: The last U.S. Coast Guard cutters and tugs that patroled New York Harbor from Governors' Island on Monday left their over 200-year-old base there.
New York City Mayor Rudolph Giuliani marked the event by criticizing the federal government's plans to sell the historic island for $500 million to help close budget gaps.

"We have to have real discussion about that," Giuliani told City Hall reporters. He added that he was interested in potential academic uses for the 172-acre site -- including proposals for New York University or Columbia University to move some of their operations there.
"But there are other ideas as well," he added, without elaborating.

A spokesman for the mayor said the Dutch Govornor of New Netherlands, Wouter Van Twiller, bought the island in 1637 from the Manhatas Indians for two axeheads, a string of beads and a few nails. The island later was taken over by the British, and occupied by their and U.S. forces during the Revolutionary War. In 1800, the island was ceded to the U.S government by New York State.

U.S. Coast Guard Chief Warrant Officer Lionel Bryant explained that the last two 65-foot tugs that sailed from Governors' Island were transferred to Bayonne, New Jersey, while a handful of cutters, which range in size from 65-feet to 120-feet, now would embark from Rosebank, Staten Island.
"We're still going to give the port the same quality of service we have for the past 207 years."

The Coast Guard is quitting the base on Governors' Island, where it at one-time had 7,000 to 8,000 personnel stationed, because it became too expensive to run the island and maintain the historic buildings, that included the stockade where Rocky Graziano, the boxer, served time for being Absent Without Leave from the U.S. Army during World War Two, according to Coast Guard and city officials.

A Coast Guard unit with about 100 personnel will stay on the island until September. After that, about 50 people, who will serve as "station-keepers" will maintain the base until its title is transferred to a new owner, Bryant said.

A New York City spokesman, who estimated the Coast Guard spent $50 to $60 million a year to maintain the site said that Washington's price tag was unreasonable, given that ongoing expense, plus the cost of running the ferries, which are the only way to get to the island, and the difficulty of building on the southern, non-historic half of the island, which is landfill.

He added that it was expected to take at least a year or so for Washington to meet environmental checks needed to ensure the base can be handed over, and let other agencies, like one for the homeless, determine whether they might like it. "We know that nobody else does," he added.
